why.say: I've written two questions on the board. The first one is, "Was it because you had no car?" The second is, "What, if anything, made it hard to get seen sooner?" Here's the rule I want you to remember from today. The only gap explanation that holds up against insurance adjusters is John Doe's own factual explanation, backed by written documents you can check: work schedules, doctor availability notes, travel logs, illness records. Your job is to draw it out with clean questions and write it down as he gives it. You don't interpret it, defend it or judge what it does to the claim. And a reason you suggested isn't his explanation at all.
why.ask: Which of those two questions would the defense rather you asked John Doe, and why?

theory.say: Here's the road for the gap interview: plan the questions only, never the answers you expect; open on the record with the date, your role and his consent; ask open questions and follow his words; ask for the paper; read it back; and record his words, with a dated task for every document. Underneath it sits one rule: coordinate, don't commingle. The medical plan and the legal claim never cross-contaminate, so your notes record facts, never conclusions, because an opinion in your notes is something the defense can use. Under A-C-T, a gap in care is a legal danger, and it routes to Atty. Thorne. Listen actively: reflect, paraphrase, then summarize. And remember privilege: a third person in the conversation can put it at risk.
theory.ask: Which of these ideas have you run into before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: Let's bring back the A-C-T Immediate Action Protocol, because the gap interview lives inside it. Assess comes first. Medical danger, like a fever or hardware failing, goes to the provider today. Legal danger, like a gap or a generic note, goes to Atty. Thorne. Then Coordinate: you clarify with the provider's office, and you remove whatever barrier the client names, whether that's transport, scheduling or a referral. Track means you document the flag and every fix you attempted that same day, and if a provider gets dropped, you write down counsel's reason. And then you're back to monitoring, because Track feeds your next check-in, where the question is simple: is the plan working?
frame.ask: Looking at John Doe's file right now, which step of A-C-T is his 14-Day Gap sitting in?

rules.say: Here are the rules for the gap call. You investigate; you don't advocate. Read the EMS report, the 02/20/2026 urgent-care history and the timeline, then write a plan that holds questions only, never the answers you expect. Run a funnel: broad open questions, follow-ups built on his words, closed questions last to pin a date or a document, one at a time. Never lead, and never judge. You know the ordinary causes, like transport, co-pays and work schedules, but you never offer them. Record only with his spoken consent, and protect privilege. If Keystone wants a Recorded Statement, he declines and sends it to us. Confirm his 03/05/2026 consult with Dr. Reyes, and ask how he'll get to care once the rental ends 03/19/2026. And the line: never tell him the gap won't matter or will hurt. Reassure the process, never the outcome.
rules.ask: If John Doe's reason is true anyway, why does it matter how you asked for it?

model.say: Have a look at this board. On the left, in green, it says ask it open. On the right, in red, never like this. Every open question sits on the same line as the leading or opinion-laden version it replaces, so you can read straight across and hear the difference. That last red row has a little UPL tag on it, and that's the soothing line, the one that sounds kind and is really an opinion on his case. Down below is the funnel: first open, then follow his words, then pin the dates and documents. Notice the pill at its mouth, recorded, consent on the record. The whole point is that the same fact, asked two ways, produces two different cases.
model.ask: Reading across the rows, which red question do you think you'd be most tempted to ask on a real call?

job.say: Now let's follow this on the job. It starts when the records show the 14-day gap. You read the EMS report, the urgent-care history and the treatment timeline in the CMS, and you save your question plan in Case Notes before the call, with no question in it naming a reason. When the call connects in the Call Simulator with AI John Doe, you state the date, who's on, and that it's recorded, and you get his consent and confirm he's somewhere private before anything substantive. If he asks what the gap does to his case, you give no opinion; you log it and escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks the same day. And if a carrier asks him for a Recorded Statement, you remind him it goes through the firm, log it in the Communications Log and tell Atty. Thorne that day.
job.ask: Where in that sequence do you think a nervous new Case Manager is most likely to slip?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues one at a time, and as soon as you think you've got it, call out Do or Don't and name the rule behind it. Some of these are the good habits: asking open, following his words and closing last, paraphrasing back so he can correct you, and preventing the next gap now, which is far cheaper than explaining a second one in the demand. Others are traps: a question that names the reason you expect, blaming him for the gap, and soothing. Watch that last one. "Don't worry" is the most common UPL slip in this module. It sounds kind, and it's an opinion on the case, the same as saying "it will hurt the case".
dodont.ask: What's the difference between telling John consistent care matters and telling him what this gap does to his case?

why.say: Before we touch a single step, I want you to know what this protocol is for, because it isn't about chasing a client. The No Contact Protocol does three jobs at once. It tracks unresponsiveness formally, it establishes due diligence before anyone ever talks about withdrawal, and it protects the firm from liability. A client who can't be reached is still a file with deadlines running on it. The protocol is the proof that the firm did its part. If you see it as just ringing someone until they pick up, you'll miss why the record matters, and the record is the whole point.
why.ask: If John Doe went quiet tomorrow, who gets hurt if nobody can prove what the firm did to reach him?

theory.say: Here's the road first: an internal review of the case status, the deadlines and the last contact; contact attempts that escalate by channel, two calls, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail, each one logged; and team notification to Atty. Thorne with what the silence puts at risk. Now the terms. An intake bottleneck is any point where the work slows or stalls, and a silent client is one. Due diligence is the proof that the firm made reasonable, documented efforts to reach the client. Approved channels are the contact methods agreed at intake, and only those count. And the emergency contact is the second person collected at intake who can still reach the client. On John Doe's file, that's Margaret Doe, his mother.
theory.ask: Which of these terms have you met before, and where would you find it on John Doe's file?

frame.say: Silence rarely comes out of nowhere, so let's look at the common intake bottlenecks behind it. There's incomplete client information, like missing contact details, incident facts or supporting documents. There's delayed follow-up: clarification requests nobody answered, verification calls missed, documents arriving slowly. Conflict checks get held up by backlog, incomplete entries or unclear opposing party details. Intake forms carry wrong dates, inconsistent statements, missing signatures or misfiled records. Sometimes the facts of loss or liability are ambiguous enough to need an attorney's review. And there are communication gaps, where an intake packet is incomplete or two departments simply talk past each other. Any one of these can turn into a client you can't reach.
frame.ask: Looking at John Doe's file right now, which of these bottlenecks do you think he's closest to?

rules.say: Step 1 is internal review, and it's the step everyone skips because they want to start dialling. Before you call anyone, check the case status, the live deadlines and the date of last contact, and confirm every earlier attempt used an approved channel. Step 2 is contact attempts, escalating: at least two phone attempts, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail or a formal letter. You escalate by channel, not by volume. Two voicemails on one number clears the phone rung and nothing more. I'll say it twice, because it matters: two voicemails, one rung. Set a follow-up reminder when a request goes out and log every attempt with date, time, channel and outcome. Step 3 is team notification and deadline impact; deadlines don't pause for silence. You can tell the client what we need and by when. You can't tell them representation will end.
rules.ask: What deadline is running on John Doe's file right now, before you pick up the phone?

model.say: Here's the whole protocol on one picture. Down the left you've got a spine of six stations. The first three are in full colour: internal review, contact attempts and team notification. That's today. Stations four to six are greyed back with a next lesson tag, so you can see where this is heading without getting ahead of ourselves. On the right, station two opens up into a ladder of channels, and each rung gets wider: phone, with two or more attempts, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail or a formal letter. And down in the corner there's a red card reminding you that the statute of limitations and hearing dates keep running the whole time.
model.ask: Why do you think each rung on that ladder is drawn wider than the one above it?

job.say: Let me tell you how this actually plays out. John Doe misses a scheduled contact or an appointment. That's your trigger. You open the Case Summary in the CMS and do Step 1: status, deadlines, last contact date, and you know the live deadlines before any outreach begins. Once that's done, you work the channel ladder in the Communications Log, two or more phone attempts, then email and text, each one logged with date, time, channel and outcome. When the ladder's exhausted, that's Step 3. You notify Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate, and you assess the impact on the file, so the escalation's documented and the SOL of 02/06/2028, plus any hearing dates, are on the record.
job.ask: What would Atty. Thorne need to see in that escalation before he could act on it?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll put up one clue at a time. When you think you know where it's going, shout Do or Don't and tell me which rule it's testing. Some rounds are good habits, like setting a follow-up reminder the moment a request goes out, or giving the client an easy way to answer, a call window, a text, an upload link. Some are traps, like letting a file sit because we're waiting on the client with nothing logged, or blaming the client for what's really a process gap. And listen for channel versus volume. It's the point people fail most often: two voicemails on the same number clears the phone rung and nothing more. Oh, and remember that emergency contact we collected at intake? This is the moment it pays off.
dodont.ask: Why does the emergency contact count as a new channel when a third call to his mobile doesn't?

why.say: The Final Warning Letter is the last low-cost step before the firm has to choose between two expensive things: spending money to find somebody, or moving to withdraw. So this letter has two jobs. It has to be specific enough that the client actually answers it, and documented enough to justify whichever of those next steps comes. And I'm going to hold you on one idea all lesson: the search waits until three things are true at the same time, not just the first one. People trigger it early all the time, and that spends the firm's money and weakens the record.
why.ask: What's the risk of spending the firm's money on a search before the letter's deadline has even passed?

theory.say: This letter closes out the outreach record. It's one last documented notice before the firm searches for the client or counsel moves to withdraw. It goes by dual delivery. Certified mail proves it was delivered, email is what actually gets a response, and each one covers the other's gap. Then there's the three-criteria gate, and I want you to hear the word gate. It's an AND gate, not a checklist, so the search waits until all three are true. The search itself is a skip-trace, a paid search for someone's current address and contacts, and because it spends firm money, counsel authorizes it. And withdrawal, ending representation by notice or motion, is decided only by the attorney, under firm and court rules.
theory.ask: Which of these have you met before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: This picks up exactly where Step 3 left off, with Steps 4 through 6. Step 4 is the Final Warning Letter. It itemizes the earlier attempts, gives a deadline of 7 to 14 days and gives notice of potential withdrawal, and it goes by certified mail and email. Step 5 is the decision point. If there's still no response, the attorney decides whether to file a Notice or a Motion to Withdraw. Step 6 is file closure. The file gets marked "No response – withdrew per protocol", and the proof of every attempt is kept. Three steps, and only one of them, the letter, is really yours to drive.
frame.ask: If John Doe went silent today, how far would his file be from Step 4?

rules.say: Step 4 goes by certified mail and email. Both, not either. The letter states the earlier attempts, gives a response deadline of 7 to 14 days and gives notice of potential withdrawal. And you confirm the address first, because a letter sent to a stale address proves nothing. At Step 5, if the client's still silent, the attorney may file a Notice of Withdrawal or a Motion to Withdraw, and that's counsel's call. Step 6 marks the file closed per protocol and keeps every proof. Skip-tracing starts only when the ladder's exhausted, the letter's gone and its deadline has passed, and counsel authorizes it with the full log attached. Meanwhile records, coverage and deadlines keep moving. The letter can state requirements and say withdrawal is possible. It can't judge the claim, advise on rights, or announce that representation's ending.
rules.ask: Why do we need both certified mail and email, when either one would technically get the letter there?

model.say: There are two panels here. On the left is the letter itself, on letterhead, with four orange badges marking what it must contain: the earlier attempts, itemized; a response deadline of 7 to 14 days; notice of potential withdrawal; and how to respond. Above it you'll see certified mail and email joined by a bold AND, because both are required. On the right is the Step 5 fork. It starts with one question: did a response come in within the deadline? If yes, the file resumes. If no, you hit a gate with three chips, the ladder exhausted, the letter sent and the deadline expired, and only then do you reach the skip-trace and the attorney's decision point. It's drawn as a gate on purpose.
model.ask: What happens on this picture if only two of those three chips are true?

job.say: Here's the story on the job. You've made your Step 3 escalation and there's still no response. That's when you draft the Final Warning Letter in the Action Plan Editor from the warning letter template, with the earlier attempts itemized and the deadline and withdrawal notice in place. Once it's ready, you confirm the current address and send it from CMS Documents, Outgoing, by certified mail and email, both channels logged and the certified receipt kept. Then the response deadline expires. Now you check that all three criteria are evidenced in the log, and only then do you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, asking for skip-trace authority and the Step 5 decision.
job.ask: What's the first thing you'd check in the log before you escalate to Atty. Thorne?

dodont.say: Now for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues, one by one. The moment you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule. You'll see good habits, like itemizing the attempts with real dates, because "we have tried several times" isn't evidence, and asking in-house help to confirm an address you can't verify. You'll also see traps, like triggering a skip-trace on the first criterion alone, or writing "we are withdrawing" in a letter the attorney never approved. That one's the hard line. The Case Manager assembles the record, and the attorney decides to withdraw. We'll come back on Day 5 for advanced skip-tracing, process servers and certified notice. Today is the trigger; Day 5 is the execution.
dodont.ask: Who decides that representation is ending, and who tells the client?

case.say: Here's what just landed on the file, dated 02/16/2026. It's file LSH-2026-MVA-770412, and there's been no client contact with John Doe for six days. His last logged contact was 02/10/2026. He missed his check-in call scheduled for 02/13/2026. The phone system shows two calls to his mobile, both ending in voicemail, and neither one is in the Communications Log. No treatment start is recorded. His emergency contact on file is Margaret Doe, at (555) 010-2291, and Step 1 of the No Contact Protocol is due today. Before we go on, would someone read the red bad entry aloud for us? "Called client, no answer." Be honest, that's what most of us would have written.
case.ask: What's missing from "called client, no answer" that a supervisor would need six months from now?

task.say: Your job is to run the No Contact Protocol on John Doe's file. Start with the Step 1 internal review in the CMS Case Summary and name the deadlines that are live right now. Don't start dialling first. Then reconstruct the attempts already made and carry the Step 2 ladder forward in the Communications Log, logging every attempt with date, time, channel and outcome, plus the next action and its due date. Part of this is a live call with Margaret Doe. Identify yourself, confirm she's the emergency contact on file, ask her to have John call the firm by a set date, and confirm his best number and current address, without disclosing any case details. What you hand in is a completed Step 1 review, an unbroken Step 2 log, and your call on whether Step 3 is warranted and what impact you'd report.
task.ask: Before you log anything, what deadline is running on this file right now?

check.say: Before you log your work, check it against these points. Did you do Step 1 first, with the status, live deadlines and last contact reviewed? Are the earlier voicemails logged with date, time and channel? Is the phone rung cleared with at least two attempts, and are email and text both tried, rather than more calls? Did you use the emergency contact? That's the rung people forget most, and we collected it at intake for exactly this. Every entry needs date, time, channel and outcome, and the next action needs a due date. Your Step 3 impact should name the SOL of 02/06/2028 and the treatment that hasn't started. That silence is what becomes the 14-Day Gap later. And nothing threatens withdrawal. Write each entry as if a supervisor will audit it six months from now.
check.ask: If you called his mobile three times, how many channels have you actually used?

case.say: This note from Atty. Thorne just landed on the file, dated 02/21/2026. He's read your Step 3 note. It's been eleven days with no word from John, and no treatment that we know of. The phone rung is cleared, emails and texts have gone out, Margaret Doe has been tried, and it's all logged. He wants the Final Warning Letter drafted for his review Monday morning: every attempt with its date, a response date, and how to reach us, by certified mail and email. Withdrawal is possible, not decided, and the letter says nothing about John's claim. Here's the hard part. You need a letter that's urgent but not threatening, and most first drafts miss one way or the other.
case.ask: What's one sentence that would make this letter sound threatening rather than urgent?

task.say: You'll draft the Step 4 Final Warning Letter to John Doe in the Action Plan Editor, using the warning letter template. Itemize the earlier attempts, and by itemize I mean list each one with its date. Set a response deadline inside the 7 to 14 day window, give notice of potential withdrawal, and tell him exactly how to respond. Every sentence stays inside the UPL boundary, so nothing on the strength of his claim, nothing on what silence does legally, and nothing announcing withdrawal as decided. Then record what has to be true before skip-tracing can start, and whose authority Step 5 needs. What you hand in is a send-ready letter with both deliveries logged and the escalation recorded.
task.ask: Whose authority does the Step 5 decision need, and where will you record that?

check.say: Before you submit, swap drafts with the person next to you and mark each other's. And first, let's read the banned and compliant pairs aloud together; it'll save you a full rewrite. Look for the firm's identification and the file reference, and the date of loss as 02/06/2026. The earlier attempts should be itemized with dates. The deadline should be an actual date inside the 7 to 14 day window, not "as soon as possible." Withdrawal should read as possible, not decided, and there should be at least two ways to respond. Certified mail and email are both recorded, with the address confirmed before sending. There's nothing about claim value or legal consequence, so no "you will lose your case." The skip-trace criteria are recorded, and Step 5 is noted as Atty. Thorne's.
check.ask: Does your partner's letter tell John what's needed and by when, without telling him what happens to his case?

questions.say: This is your Knowledge Check. Your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. You'll set out all six steps of the No Contact Protocol in order, with what's required at each one. You'll state the protocol's three purposes and say which one protects the firm rather than the client. A word on that second question: it's easy to answer shallowly. Protection from liability is the purpose people leave out, and it's exactly why the record gets built the way it does. Then there's a colleague who logged three voicemails on three days and called the ladder exhausted. Tell me what's wrong and what the log should show.
questions.ask: Which of the three purposes do you think is the easiest one to forget?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary, where you put the principles in your own words. Here's the scenario. It's 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab reports John Doe has missed two visits. Keystone ended Margaret's rental on 03/19, his carpool ended 04/01, and Dana Whitfield has asked John for a Recorded Statement. Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each step protects. This one pulls it all together: the running SOL, a Treatment Gap that's hardening, and the claims work that has to keep moving anyway. Keep in mind, too, that the gap you're watching build here is the same 14 days defense counsel will ask John Doe about at his deposition on Day 5.
summary.ask: Of those three problems, which one protects the most if you deal with it first?

scale.say: Last step is your Skill Scale. Rate yourself honestly, one to five, on each competency, then submit it for review. One to five isn't a grade. It's a picture of where you actually are today. When I get these back, I'll compare your self-rating with your Knowledge Check score, and wherever there's a wide gap, either way, you and I will have a short conversation about it. Overrating and underrating both tell me something useful.
scale.ask: Which competency here are you least sure how to rate, and why?

why.say: Let me start with a date: 04/07/2026. Does anyone know what was due that day on John Doe's file? It was his week-6 mark of care. And John Doe wasn't there. Here's why that matters. On an LOP, nobody denies the next six visits in real time. Keystone does it later, at the demand, by calling the care unnecessary or the injury minor. That leaves you as the only real-time check that John Doe's plan is working, and the person who acts the very day it isn't.
why.ask: On an LOP file, who denies unnecessary care, and when, and what does that make you?

map.say: Here's the road for monitoring treatment, before we get into it. You check in on visits, pain, function and any barrier. When something's off, you name the variance: clinical, psychosocial or systemic. Then you run A-C-T. Assess, where medical danger goes to the provider and legal danger goes to Atty. Thorne. Coordinate, where you clarify with the office and remove the barrier. And Track, where every fix attempt goes into a GIRP note, facts only. Five steps, and you'll use them on John Doe's file more than once.

theory.say: Knowing the Standard Treatment Map is what separates a Case Manager who watches a recovery from one who drives it, because deviations are what trigger denials and IMEs. The acute phase is days 1 to 14, with the ER, imaging, initial PT and documenting causation. Sub-acute runs weeks 2 to 8, with active PT, specialists and measured functional gains. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24, with injections, work hardening and barriers to returning to work, and after that comes maintenance, with home exercise and as-needed visits. Maximum Medical Improvement is the provider's finding that more care won't improve things. It closes treatment and opens pre-demand. When a client drifts off the map, variance analysis asks why first: is it clinical, psychosocial or systemic, and you ask before funding stops.
theory.ask: Which phase do you think John Doe was in when he missed his week-6 mark?

theory2.say: A few more ideas you'll lean on. The A-C-T protocol is your immediate action for any red flag: you Assess the danger, Coordinate the fix and Track it, and that documentation is what gives counsel his why. "Reasonable and necessary" is the utilization-review test. Is the care common for this mechanism of injury, and is there objective functional gain, not just subjective pain? SMART goals, meaning specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, like the week-6 measures, are what hold up with clinicians and adjusters alike. And there's the stakeholder triad of clinical, legal and financial loops, with you as the router. One broken loop can stall a case for months.
theory2.ask: What would a SMART goal for John Doe's next six weeks of PT actually sound like?

frame.say: Here's the Standard Treatment Map phase by phase. Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER, MRI or CT, bracing, RICE and initial PT, while we establish causation and PIP coverage. Sub-acute is weeks 2 to 8, with active PT two or three times a week and specialist follow-up. That's where the week-6 check lives, looking for 20 to 30 percent better range of motion. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24, covering work hardening, injections, psychological adjustment and finding the barriers to return to work. Maintenance comes after week 24, with home exercise and as-needed visits while we watch for the provider's MMI finding. MMI is the endpoint. Treatment closes, and the pre-demand audit opens.
frame.ask: On 04/08/2026, day 61 of John Doe's file, where on this map is he sitting?

rules.say: Monitor outcomes, not just attendance. Ask about visits, pain and what he can't do at work or home, and hunt the barriers, internal ones like fear or mood and external ones like transport or money. On 04/08/2026, day 61, he's in week 9. At every check-in, ask whether he's improving. His week-6 mark fell on 04/07/2026, which is 02/24/2026 plus 42 days, and the next step, whether that's medication, injections or a specialist, is the provider's decision. Name the variance before you fix it. Run A-C-T for every red flag, and adjust the plan first, because it's usually the plan, not the client. Climb the ladder one documented rung at a time: clinical, then administrative, then legal. Write every intervention as a GIRP note. And you coordinate care, you never direct it. Never tell him to skip treatment, or that missed visits cut his claim.
rules.ask: Why does writing "this will help the case" in a GIRP note put the file at risk?

model.say: This picture shows how A-C-T fits inside monitoring rather than beside it. There's a navy ring with the question "Is the plan working?" in the middle. Down at about four o'clock, a red detect node breaks out into three steps: assess, coordinate, track. Then notice the arrow from track. It curves right back up into the ring. Up in the corner is the treatment map, with a marker on restorative, week 9, 04/08/2026. And on the left are the three variance chips, clinical, psychosocial and systemic, with psychosocial lit up, because what's derailed John is that he's got no transport. A-C-T isn't a detour from monitoring. It closes back into it.
model.ask: Why is psychosocial the variance that's highlighted for John Doe, rather than clinical or systemic?

job.say: Let's walk through a few weeks of this file. A provider's missed-visit alert comes in. That same day, you call AI John Doe, classify the variance and write the GIRP note in Case Notes, dated the day the alert arrived. At week 6, 04/07/2026, you ask the provider for the re-evaluation measures: range of motion, pain score and disability index. Whether a PHQ-9 or GAD-7 screen is indicated is the provider's call, and anything putting his mental health in the record gets flagged to Atty. Thorne. If the barrier isn't fixed at the clinical rung, you climb one rung with a written notice to the carrier causing it, copied to Atty. Thorne, and only property facts to Keystone PD, with each rung dated. Red flags that can cost the claim go to Atty. Thorne with the fix you attempted.
job.ask: Why does the GIRP note need to be dated the day the alert arrives, not the day you finish?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues come up one at a time, and when you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule. You'll be watching for red flags to raise with the provider, like more than 12 sessions with no gain, passive-only care, or two or more missed visits. You'll see yellow flags reported with a plan, in the map's language. Then there's proofreading laterality, because everything on this file is right-sided, and recording a disruption the day it happens, so it never needs the reconstruction the 14-Day Gap does. The traps are continuing the plan unchanged through a crisis, blaming John, or jumping to Atty. Thorne before the clinical and administrative rungs. And remember, the middle step is Coordinate, but it still opens with that clarifying call to the provider's office.
dodont.ask: What argument from the defense does a factual A-C-T record answer later on?

why.say: I've got John Doe's PIP Log up, with the right-hand column covered. Harbor Point has paid $685.00, $640.00, $2,395.00 and then $640.00 for the 03/27/2026 visit. How much PIP is left? Take a second. It's $640.00. If you can't keep that column straight, you can't decide an LOP request. Treatment is the file's engine room, and somebody has to pay for it while the claim is open. On this file three payers stand in a default order: Harbor Point PIP, then Peach State, then a Letter of Protection. An LOP issued out of order turns a bill an earlier payer would have paid into a lien against John Doe's net.
why.ask: How much PIP does John Doe have left after the 03/27/2026 visit?

theory.say: Once the claim's set up, the Case Plan runs on three pillars: clinical care, functional status and subrogation management, and that last one decides who pays. The Payer Order is the default sequence. MedPay or PIP pays first, then health insurance, and an LOP comes last. Keeping that order keeps the liens down. PIP is first-party coverage for Medical Bills regardless of fault, up to its limit, and unlike PIP it never pays wages. Health insurance pays covered care at its contract rate, but it may hold a reimbursement right against the recovery. A Letter of Protection is the client's signed agreement that a provider gets paid from any recovery, which makes it a consensual lien on his net.
theory.ask: Which of these payers have you dealt with before, and which one is first in line on John Doe's file?

theory2.say: The other half of the theory is about keeping care moving. The Standard Treatment Map is the usual route: emergency, imaging, chiropractic and PT, orthopedics, pain management, sometimes surgery, and every stop needs a payer. Monitoring progress means evaluating clinical and functional outcomes, not ticking boxes, so you ask about the plan, not just "How are you?" Crisis intervention is stepping in when care gets denied or stalled by bureaucracy, and you adjust the plan to the immediate issue first. And watch for medication red flags, like an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, or doses climbing with no new diagnosis. You don't judge that yourself. You raise it with the provider.
theory2.ask: Instead of asking John Doe how he is, what would you ask him about his plan?

frame.say: Let's set the Payer Order out step by step. First you identify the payers, listing every source and its default order, and remember that who's actually primary is Atty. Thorne's call. Next is MedPay or PIP, which is first-party, regardless of fault, up to its limit, and PIP also pays 80% of lost income, where MedPay pays Medical Bills only. Then comes the Health Plan, which pays covered care at its contract rate but may assert a reimbursement right against the recovery. The Letter of Protection is the last rung, for care the earlier payers can't carry. It's paid from any recovery, on Atty. Thorne's terms.
frame.ask: Where is John Doe on this ladder for his Riverton Spine & Rehab physical therapy?

rules.say: In treatment, the question becomes "Is the plan working?" and you're facilitating, coordinating and advocating. Run the Payer Order: Harbor Point PIP, then Peach State, then an LOP. John claims the $5,000 PIP as a passenger in Kevin Alvarez's 2020 Ford Escape, because no policy in his household carries PIP. PIP pays in date order, never wages. When Crescent Pain & Spine billed Peach State on 05/15/2026 with $640.00 of PIP left, you tracked both ledgers and never re-routed a paid claim. Riverton Spine & Rehab got an LOP because it's out of network. Summit Imaging's 03/11/2026 MRI went to PIP, since every needless LOP is a lien on his net. LOP terms are Atty. Thorne's, so you prepare, route, transmit once he approves and confirm receipt. Never promise a provider an amount, a reduction or a date, and never explain John's liability to him.
rules.ask: Riverton and Summit Imaging both asked for an LOP. Why did only one of them get it?

model.say: Here's the PIP Log, Harbor Point's $5,000, with five rows paid in date order. Above it there's a gauge draining in five steps, and the last one lands on $0.00 at 06/12/2026, in red. On the left is the payer rail: PIP first, Peach State second, and the LOP third, stamped counsel-approved terms. Then look at the two provider chips along the bottom. Riverton Spine & Rehab has a tick for its LOP. Summit Imaging has a cross, because its bill went to PIP instead. That's the argument of the whole slide. An LOP is the last rung of the Payer Order, not the first answer to a provider who asks.
model.ask: What would a $2,395.00 LOP for Summit Imaging have cost John Doe at the end?

job.say: Picture a normal month on this file. A provider asks for an LOP. You run the Payer Order and prepare one on counsel's template only for care PIP and Peach State can't carry, then route it for approval from CMS Documents, Outgoing. The payer check is recorded first, and nothing goes out without Atty. Thorne. When PIP pays a bill, you post the payment, the running total and the balance on the PIP Log, and it ties to Harbor Point, hitting $5,000.00 on the 06/12/2026 visit. When an LOP statement arrives, you update the LOP register and check every line, so through 04/02/2026 that's 16 visits at $185.00, or $2,960.00, all attended. For a new referral, you do a warm handoff with John on the line and confirm the payer before the first visit.
job.ask: If Riverton bills a date John Doe didn't attend, what do you do with that line?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues in turn. Call Do or Don't as soon as you can, and name the rule. Good habits on this one include asking "Is the plan working?" at every contact, ending each call by asking what might get in the way of treatment this week, reconciling conflicting provider notes straight away, and telling John which payer handles which bill, because cost worry left unanswered is how a client stops going. The traps are issuing an LOP just because a provider asked, telling a provider they'll be paid in full at settlement, mission creep, and handing Atty. Thorne raw records with no summary. And remember, an LOP isn't free. Every dollar on it is one Day 4 has to negotiate.
dodont.ask: Why is an LOP never really free for John Doe, even when the provider is happy with it?

why.say: Before we look at the slide, take out RS26, Peach State's Explanation of Benefits, and let's read it together, column by column. So, what does John Doe owe Crescent? Find the bottom line. The EOB says $0.00. Every payer reports what it did with a bill. Peach State does it in an EOB, and Harbor Point does it in its PIP payment history. Read line by line, they tell you what was billed, what was paid, what was written off and what John Doe may still owe. Those documents are the proof behind the Medical Specials, behind every lien amount, and behind every answer you give a provider or John Doe about a balance.
why.ask: Reading RS26, what does John Doe actually owe Crescent Pain & Spine for the injection?

theory.say: Every payer reports back on a bill, the Health Plan in an Explanation of Benefits and PIP in its payment history, and you read both before you ever touch a lien. An EOB is the plan's account of one processed claim. It's not a bill; it's proof of who paid what. Billed versus allowed is the first thing to see. Billed is the provider's charge, allowed is the plan's fee schedule, and in network the gap gets written off. Remark codes are the short codes explaining each line. CO-45 is the fee-schedule write-off, and AC1 flags a possible accident. And member responsibility, meaning the deductible, copay and coinsurance, is the most an in-network provider may bill the patient.
theory.ask: Which of these terms have you seen on your own Medical Bills, and what did it mean there?

theory2.say: Four more ideas round this out. Balance billing is when a provider bills the patient for a contractual write-off. In network that isn't allowed, so it's an error, not a lien. The PIP payment history is the carrier's ledger of every check, showing the date of service, the amount paid and the limit remaining. Exhaustion is what happens once that limit's spent. Later bills come back unpaid, and you route them to the next payer. And reconciliation is matching every provider balance to each payer's EOB or check, so that no bill that's already been paid ever turns into a lien against John Doe.
theory2.ask: If a provider bills John Doe for a write-off, is that a lien, a debt or an error?

frame.say: Here's how you read an EOB, top to bottom, every time. First, match the claim: the member ID, claim number, provider and date of service against the CMS treatment record. Then go from billed to allowed, which means the charge, the plan's allowed amount and the contractual adjustment it wrote off. Next is the patient's share, the deductible, copay and coinsurance, because member responsibility is the most a provider may bill. After that comes what the plan paid, with its date and its EFT or check number, since that's where any reimbursement claim starts. Read the remark codes: CO-45 explains the write-off, and AC1 flags an accident and the plan's reimbursement right. Finally, reconcile and log it against the provider's statement and the lien register, and flag any balance billing.
frame.ask: Which step in reading an EOB do you think people skip most often?

rules.say: Peach State's EOB of 06/03/2026, claim PS-2605-449021, covers Crescent's 05/15/2026 epidural injection, and it says THIS IS NOT A BILL. Crescent billed $3,400.00 and the plan allowed $1,860.00. The $1,540.00 difference is Crescent's write-off. The plan paid $1,860.00, and member responsibility is $0.00. CO-45 explains that write-off, and AC1 is how Peach State's reimbursement right attaches. Now turn to Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement asking John Doe for $1,540.00. That's a balance bill, not a debt and not a lien. You document it, route it to Atty. Thorne that day, draft a correction request and tell John what's happening. Peach State's claim starts at $1,860.00, never $3,400.00, and you route its accident questionnaire to Atty. Thorne. Harbor Point's five checks total $5,000.00, exhausted 06/26/2026. You read and reconcile; whether he owes anything is counsel's call.
rules.ask: Crescent's $1,540.00 statement: is it a lien we missed, or a bill nobody owes?

model.say: We've got two documents side by side, each read line by line. On the left is Peach State's EOB for claim PS-2605-449021, with that red stamp, THIS IS NOT A BILL. It has six rows: billed $3,400.00, allowed $1,860.00, the $1,540.00 adjustment, $0.00 deductible, $1,860.00 paid, and $0.00 member responsibility. Each orange tag tells you where that number goes on the file. On the right is Harbor Point's payment history, five checks with a limit bar falling from $5,000.00 to nothing, stamped exhausted 06/26/2026. And underneath is Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement for $1,540.00, with a dashed line back to that $0.00 row and a question: balance bill?
model.ask: Which row on Peach State's EOB is the most Crescent may bill John Doe?

job.say: Let's run this as it happens on the file. An EOB arrives, and you post billed, allowed, adjustment, paid and member share against the visit in CMS Liens and Documents, so the $1,860.00 plan payment is logged and claim PS-2605-449021 is linked to the visit. A PIP check clears, and you post it on the PIP Log with the date of service and the limit remaining, until it ties to Harbor Point's history with $0.00 left after 06/26/2026. Then a patient statement shows a balance. You compare it with the EOB's member responsibility, flag the $1,540.00, tell Atty. Thorne the same day and draft the correction request. And when Peach State's itemized lien arrives, you match each line to an EOB and to the collision, so only those lines stand.
job.ask: What would you do with a line on Peach State's lien that no EOB supports?

dodont.say: Here comes 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues one by one; call Do or Don't and name the rule. The good habits are reading every EOB down to member responsibility before you answer a balance question, asking each provider for an itemized statement showing every payer's credit, keeping billed and paid on the same CMS line, and telling John what you're doing and when he'll hear back. The traps are logging a lien at the billed amount instead of what the plan paid, treating a write-off as something he owes, and sending a bill to PIP after it was exhausted on 06/26/2026. One number to hold onto: Peach State can claim back $1,860.00, never $3,400.00. You read, reconcile and report. Whether John Doe owes a balance is Atty. Thorne's call.
dodont.ask: After Harbor Point's $0.00 line on 06/26/2026, where does the next bill go?

why.say: The adjuster says the gap proves John Doe healed. What would you collect? Call it out and I'll write it up. Good. Now let's sort that list into two boxes. Remember the rule: the only gap explanation that holds up against adjusters is John Doe's own factual explanation, backed by written documents you can check. Around it, records made at the time do the rest: provider notes that place onset at the collision, histories that agree, the EMS report and the work records, and later a causation opinion Atty. Thorne requests. Anything in the other box, a record made to order, destroys the very case it was meant to save.
why.ask: Which item on our list would an adjuster find hardest to argue with, and why?

theory.say: You need to understand the why behind the paperwork, and here it is: continuity is proved by what the record already shows, never by what it's asked to say. Continuity of care is an unbroken path along the Standard Treatment Map, each step following from the last, and that chain is exactly what an adjuster tests. A Treatment Gap is any break in it, before the first treatment or midstream, and adjusters read it as minor, healed or unrelated. Records made at the time, written by EMS, providers and employers as things happened, are your strongest proof, because nobody wrote them for the claim. And consistent histories, repeating the same mechanism, onset and body region across charts, are what make continuity believable.
theory.ask: Who on John Doe's file wrote something down about his neck before anyone thought about a claim?

theory2.say: Four more ideas. A causation opinion is a treating doctor's opinion linking the injury to the collision. It's the bridge across a gap, and Atty. Thorne requests it. Record integrity means a record changes only by its author's dated addendum. Altering one can be evidence tampering or fraud. Excuse notes prove only what their author saw or ordered at a visit, so days nobody examined him need other proof. And generic notes, ones that don't tie the complaints to the collision, weaken causation. Under A-C-T, those get flagged to Atty. Thorne. You don't fix them yourself.
theory2.ask: What proves John Doe couldn't work 02/09 through 02/13, when no doctor saw him?

frame.say: These are the treatment red flags, and for each one there's a reason the defense loves it. In physical therapy, watch for more than 12 sessions with no gain and no specialist or imaging suggested, which reads as a stalled plan or over-treatment. Passive care only, heat packs, TENS and massage with no active exercise, is feel-good care adjusters discount. Two or more missed appointments let the defense say the injury wasn't serious enough to treat. Surgery recommended before PT or injections, outside an emergency, invites a reasonable-and-necessary challenge. In pain management, an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, with doses rising and the diagnosis unchanged, is a safety risk. And in records, left and right switched, or notes about life stress instead of the collision, weaken both credibility and causation.
frame.ask: Which of these red flags do you see on John Doe's file right now?

rules.say: Continuity is proved by records made at the time, then by a doctor's opinion that reads them, and never by explanations made to order. Read every history for mechanism, the collision, onset on 02/06/2026, and region, the neck and right arm, since the 2021 visits were low back. If the PT notes and Dr. Reyes disagree, flag it to Atty. Thorne that day. Never ask a provider to change, back-date or add to a record, and never order an excuse note. For 02/09 to 02/13, Northgate's Attendance Record is the proof. The EMS report bridges day zero, so record "declined transport" exactly as written. Keep the 02/07/2026 Riverton Drug receipt and the full text thread to Margaret Doe. A causation opinion is Atty. Thorne's request; you assemble and track, never draft. Tell providers scheduling facts only, and never hide an interruption.
rules.ask: Riverton's front desk offers to add a line saying the pain began at the crash. What do you say, and who do you tell?

model.say: This is a compare board, and the heading says it all: made at the time versus made to order. On the left, under a green rule, is what counts, each document with its date: the 02/06 EMS report, the 02/07 receipt, the 02/09 to 02/13 call-outs, the 02/20 urgent care note and the 06/19 Causation Letter. On the right, in red, is what never happens, every item struck through. Now look along the bottom. There's a timeline from 02/06 to 06/19 with the left card's documents pinned onto it, so you can see the proof was being laid down while the gap was actually happening. That's the point. Timing is what makes a document believable.
model.ask: Why does the 06/19 Causation Letter belong in the left column, even though it came months later?

job.say: Here's the rhythm on the job. A provider record arrives, and you compare its mechanism, onset date and body region with the other histories on the treatment timeline. Either it's logged consistent, or it's flagged with the conflicting line quoted. If one history conflicts with another provider's, you flag it to Atty. Thorne through Tasks that same day, and you don't contact the provider about the wording or request a change. When Atty. Thorne decides to seek a causation opinion, you assemble the records for his letter and docket the follow-up, so it goes under his signature with the date on the calendar. And when a work or excuse note arrives, you check the signer, the date and the covered days against the visit record, flagging any mismatch.
job.ask: Why shouldn't you call the provider yourself to sort out a conflicting history?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. One clue at a time, and the moment you know, call Do or Don't and name the rule. The good habits are collecting what already exists before asking for anything new, quoting records exactly, flagging conflicting statements rather than fixing them, and keeping every interruption visible on the timeline with its dates. The traps include asking a provider to "clarify" a note in a way that tells them what to write, and leaving the gap off the timeline and hoping nobody notices. And here's one that catches people. A stronger note isn't always better. A note that shows up after the firm asked for it, saying exactly what the firm needed, is the weakest document in the file.
dodont.ask: Why would your fingerprints on Dr. Reyes's wording make her letter worthless?

case.say: We'll run this in two passes, one for each date. The first is 02/23/2026, and this email just came in from Tammy Greer, Office Manager at Riverton Spine & Rehab. John Doe is booked for his chiropractic and PT evaluation tomorrow, 02/24, they're out of network with Peach State, and they want a signed Letter of Protection and his HIPAA authorization today. Thorne for approval and signature, and transmit it with the claim-specific HIPAA authorization, asking for itemized statements and a missed-visit alert. Open on the record with the date, who's on the call, your role, his consent to recording, and that he can talk privately. John says he isn't going. It's too far, he's got no ride out there, and somebody at work told him the place is out of network with Peach State. He still wants the appointment. Where he goes, among the options his doctors find appropriate, is his choice, and what care he gets is Dr. Reyes's and the treating provider's call, so you give no medical advice at all. Check Crescent's network status with Peach State yourself. Thorne, and the attendance check after 05/15/2026.

Calling John back, reading Dr. Reyes's referral, verifying Crescent with Peach State, booking 05/15/2026 with John on the line, the calendar, the Parties entry, the Peach State billing and the Lien Tracker flag, transport, the GIRP note and the report are all done on 04/22/2026. And the attendance check on 05/18/2026 stays on my own list.

Did you verify Crescent's network status with Peach State, instead of repeating what he heard at work? Crescent Pain & Spine, Dr. Omar Haddad, is in network for member PSH-55017742. case.say: I'm putting the adjuster's four arguments on the board: not serious, recovered early, treatment unnecessary, another cause. Your record is going to answer each one with a document, not a sentence. Here's what landed on 06/22/2026. John Doe reached MMI on 06/12/2026, and Dr. Alana Reyes's Causation Letter of 06/19/2026 is in.
