Atty. Thorne wants the Gap Explanation Record before the pre-demand session, with both interruptions at exact dates, every reason beside its dated document, "account only" where there isn't one, and a defense-eye pass first.
case.ask: Which of the adjuster's four arguments does Dr. Reyes's letter answer most directly?

task.say: You'll build John Doe's Gap Explanation Record in the CMS Case File. It covers both interruptions with exact dates: the 14-day gap, 02/06 to 02/20/2026, and the 19-day disruption, 04/02 to 04/21/2026. Pair every reason with the dated document that backs it up, and mark any reason with no independent document as "account only". Cite the complaints before and after each interruption, and the firm's follow-up during the disruption. Write facts and citations only, so no argument, no valuation, and nothing quoted from the privileged call. Run your defense-eye pass, then route it to Atty. Thorne through Tasks. What you hand in is a routed record, ready for him to decide how it's used in the demand.
task.ask: Which reason on this file has the weakest document, and what do you do about it?

model.say: Here's the shape the record takes. It's one CMS card, Gap Explanation Record, John Doe, split into two bands of equal weight. The top band is the 14-day gap, 02/06 to 02/20/2026. The bottom band is the 19-day disruption, 04/02 to 04/21/2026. Each band has three columns: the reason, the corroborating document and the date. Any row that rests only on John's word gets a grey "account only" tag, and down in the corner is the control to route it to Atty. Thorne. Notice that the second interruption gets exactly the same room as the first. Every reason sits beside its proof, in both bands.
model.ask: Why do you think the 19-day band is drawn exactly as big as the 14-day one?

check.say: Now check your record. The 14-day gap runs 02/06 to 02/20/2026, and the 19-day disruption runs 04/02 to 04/21/2026, with missed visits on 04/03, 04/07, 04/09 and 04/14. For no transportation, you've got the tow record and Keystone's rental from 02/18/2026, with Kevin Alvarez's Escape in the shop marked account only. For expecting it to pass, there's the 02/07/2026 Riverton Drug receipt and the texts to Margaret Doe. The cost worry gets Peach State's 02/01/2026 eligibility, with the worry itself account only. The urgent-care note is quoted exactly. Did you show the firm's follow-up from 04/08? And don't stop at the 14-day gap. The 19-day disruption needs the same record: his reasons, each beside its document. Keep the work-product layer in the CMS, and keep the privileged call out of everything.
check.ask: What's the difference between this internal record and a gap timeline that goes to Keystone?

questions.say: Here's your Knowledge Check. Answer from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. You'll read Peach State's 06/03/2026 EOB for claim PS-2605-449021 line by line and say where each amount goes. You'll handle Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement asking John Doe for $1,540.00. And you'll explain from the Payer Order why Riverton got an LOP on 02/23/2026 and Summit's 03/11/2026 request was declined. Then there's a pressure scenario later in the check. The right answer promises nothing new, points the office manager to the LOP signed on 02/23/2026, and gets Atty. Thorne involved before the appointment.
questions.ask: What may you tell Summit Imaging when you decline its LOP request, and what may you not?

summary.say: Now write your Self-Summary. It's 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab reports John Doe has missed two visits, Keystone ended Margaret's rental on 03/19, his carpool ended 04/01, and Dana Whitfield has asked John for a Recorded Statement. Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each step protects. A couple of things I'll be looking for. On the 2021 visits, documenting low back versus neck, resolved, no prior neck complaints, is proof; saying they "don't matter" is arguing. On medication red flags, the provider hears the safety issue, Atty. Thorne hears the legal one, and you document the conversation.
summary.ask: Which of these three problems would you hand to Atty. Thorne before anything else today?

scale.say: Finish with your Skill Scale. Rate each competency from one to five, honestly, and submit it for review. I'll be comparing your self-rating with your score, and if there's a wide gap, we'll talk it through together. One thing to know before you rate yourself: UPL works as a gate. A strong score doesn't survive a single payment promise to a provider, so if you made one anywhere today, rate with that in mind.
scale.ask: Where do you think your self-rating and your score will be furthest apart?

questions.say: Before the written check, let's do question 3 out loud. I'll be John Doe, and one of you is the Case Manager. I'm going to ask you, "Is this gap going to wreck my case?" and if I hear "don't worry", I'm stopping us right there. Then write your answers from this file, in your own words. Name the four reasons for the 14-day gap, each with its corroborating document and date. Rewrite "Was it because you had no car?" so it surfaces the same reason without suggesting it, and explain what the leading version costs. Question 2 matters most here, so take your time with it.
questions.ask: Who wants to be the Case Manager first while I play John Doe?

summary.say: Time for your Self-Summary. Same date, 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab says John Doe has missed two visits, Keystone ended Margaret's rental on 03/19, his carpool ended 04/01, and Dana Whitfield wants a Recorded Statement from him. What do you do first, second and third, and what does each step protect? While you're thinking about records, here's something to chew on. Why is a provider's offer to add a line to a chart more dangerous than a missing note? A missing note is a weakness. An altered one is a credibility collapse, and possibly a fraud question.
summary.ask: Why is a provider's offer to change a record more dangerous than a note that's simply missing?

scale.say: Last up is the Skill Scale. Give yourself a one to five on each competency and submit it for review. I'll compare each rating with your score and talk through any big gap with you. And remember UPL is a gate here too. A strong score doesn't survive a coached answer or a requested change to a record. If you couldn't rewrite that leading question cleanly, be honest about it; it just means another round in the simulator.
scale.ask: Which skill from today would you most want another run at in the simulator?

why.say: The demand goes out later today, but what it can claim gets decided right here. Pre-demand is where most of a file's value is won or lost, because The demands that follow can only spend what this audit proves. One duplicate line or one unchecked limit is Keystone's easy out. Now try this arithmetic. There's $7,965.00 in liens waiting behind a $10,000 BI limit. Take a moment and work out what's left before John Doe sees anything from that layer. That's why every dollar in this audit has to be right.
why.ask: With $7,965.00 in liens behind a $10,000 BI limit, how much of that layer is left?

theory.say: Think of the full pre-demand audit as the final stress test, the point where we stop collecting information and start using it, leaving the defense zero easy outs. It starts with the trinity of case alignment: narrative, physicality and medicals must all agree, and if one's out of line, the value collapses. Maximum Medical Improvement is the provider's finding that care has plateaued. The incurred Specials are complete, and the audit can begin. Special damages are Medical Bills plus lost wages plus Property Damage, the provable dollar loss, and every line needs a document. And the medical and billing audit runs three passes, chronology for gaps, coding for duplicates and prior history for pre-existing conditions, so we find the weak spots first.
theory.ask: Which of these audit ideas is new to you, and which part of John Doe's file would it test first?

theory2.say: Four more pieces. Liens and subrogation come first. Health Plans, government payers and LOP providers may all claim repayment from the recovery, and every lien shrinks his net. The Property Damage deep dive looks at photos of the point of impact, the estimate against the final bill and any supplements, because Property Damage proves the force behind the injury. The defense-eye audit is reading the file the way the adjuster will, looking at social media, a minor-impact label and the venue, and naming each value killer. And policy-limits targets are the verified limits in the order they open. That's what each policy can pay, which isn't the same thing as what the claim's worth.
theory2.ask: What on John Doe's file would an adjuster point to for a minor-impact argument?

frame.say: This is the Master Audit Checklist. On the financial side you've got special damages, meaning Medical Bills, lost wages and Property Damage, every line documented. Lost wages need the employer's wage letter plus a provider's work note, and without both they're usually rejected. Then lien resolution, covering every subrogation interest, whether statutory, Health Plan or a consensual LOP. For liability proof, there's the final report, witness contact and any drift in their statements, and whether the physics is even possible. The Property Damage deep dive checks that the point of impact is clear and that supplements show hidden structural damage. And medical and billing gets the chronology with every gap explained, coding with no duplicates, and five to ten years of history.
frame.ask: Which line of this checklist do you think is weakest on John Doe's file today?

rules.say: Who decides John reached MMI? Not you, and not John. It's Lakeside Orthopedics, recorded from its 06/12/2026 note with the future-care plan. Audit for verification, valuation, risk and compliance, with the SOL of 02/06/2028 docketed. The Civic runs on its own Keystone PD claim, so his BI Specials are medical plus wages. Three passes: chronology for the 14 days and the 19-day disruption, coding for duplicates, and prior history, the 2021 low-back visits. Show billed beside paid, because that choice is Atty. Thorne's. Northgate verifies 9 shifts at 8 hours and $22.00, so $1,584.00, and flag the five shifts with no note. The $3,400 to $6,800 in future injections stays out of the total. Register every lien, including Peach State's $1,860.00. $16,401.40 already exceeds the $10,000 limit. You audit, total and flag; you don't value the case.
rules.ask: Who decides that John Doe reached MMI, and where do you record it from?

model.say: Read this one left to right. First there's a gate, MMI on 06/12/2026, with a green tick. Nothing enters the ledger until that's passed. In the centre is the ledger itself. See the Riverton Spine & Rehab row: $6,290.00 is struck through in red and replaced by $6,105.00, with a badge flagging a $185.00 duplicate on 05/04/2026. That's what the coding pass catches. Underneath is the sum, $14,817.40 in medicals plus $1,584.00 in wages, which gives $16,401.40. The future medical card sits deliberately outside the frame, in the narrative. On the right are the targets in the order they open: $10,000 BI, $20,000 Host UM and $10,000 Relative UM, each with its source.
model.ask: What would Keystone have done with that $185.00 duplicate if we hadn't caught it?

job.say: The story starts on 06/12/2026, when the MMI note arrives. You record MMI and the future-care plan on the treatment timeline and open the pre-demand audit as a task with an owner and a date. As the final bills and records come in, you build the Specials ledger and reconcile it against the chronology until every billed date matches a visit and the medical total is $14,817.40. Once the ledger's reconciled, you register every lien and record billed beside paid in the Liens and the Net Sheet's Lien Tracker. That means $1,860.00 and $6,105.00 are listed and the billed-versus-paid question is routed to Atty. Thorne. Finally, before the ask, you re-verify each limit in the Coverage Matrix: $10,000, then $20,000, then $10,000, $40,000 in all, each with its written source.
job.ask: Why re-verify the limits now, when the Coverage Matrix was confirmed weeks ago?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal the clues one at a time; call Do or Don't and name the rule as soon as you see it. The good habits are stress-testing the file before the defense does, locking in total damages and then protecting them by finding every lien before the demand, and recording the source of every figure so Atty. Thorne can check any line in seconds. The traps are sending the demand and hoping nobody checks the math, padding the Specials with future care, and finding a lien after the release is signed. Watch billed versus paid, too. Picking a column yourself or hiding the paid one are both wrong, so show both and route the choice.
dodont.ask: Why doesn't the Civic's repair ever count toward the $40,000 or the BI Specials?

why.say: Let me read you two first lines. One: "On 02/06/2026 John Doe was a front-seat passenger…" Two: "John Doe is at MMI with $16,401.40 in audited Specials against a $10,000 BI limit, and I need your decisions." Which of those can Atty. Thorne actually act on? Right, the second. He makes the strategy calls from your brief, and that's why its shape matters so much. A brief that opens with the chronology buries the decision. One that hides a risk misleads him. And one that makes the call for him crosses a line that isn't yours to cross.
why.ask: Which of those two opening lines could Atty. Thorne act on in the first ten seconds?

theory.say: A pre-demand audit is the file's sanity check, and the strategy brief carries its findings, not conclusions, to Atty. Thorne, who makes every call. The brief reports on each of the core audit objectives: verification, valuation, risk and compliance. It flags statement drift, which is a witness whose story changes between tellings, because drift is an opening for the defense. It names the value killers the defense-eye audit turned up, such as social media, a minor-impact label or the venue, and counsel weighs each one. And it always carries the lien totals, because when the math is wrong or a lien gets missed, you end up with a short-funded settlement where the client takes home nothing.
theory.ask: What would a short-funded settlement mean for John Doe, in plain terms?

frame.say: The brief rests on the four core objectives of the pre-demand audit. Verification asks whether the facts match the physical evidence, meaning the photos, the Police Report and the scene. Valuation asks whether the damages are calculated accurately, with the bills, the wages and the future care each justified by a document. Risk assessment covers the weak spots the defense will argue: comparative negligence, social media, a minor-impact label, venue. And compliance means every statutory requirement is met before the demand issues, the Statute of Limitations first. If you can report a finding under each of those four, you're ready to brief.
frame.ask: Under which of these four objectives does John Doe's file still have an open question?

rules.say: Lead with the bottom line in one sentence: MMI 06/12/2026, $16,401.40 in audited Specials against a $10,000 BI limit, decisions needed before any demand is drafted. Next come the facts, audited and sourced, with the narrative, physicality and medicals agreeing. That includes report RPD-26-018842, Smith cited for failure to stop, Ruth Calloway checked for drift, and the doorbell video. On force, John's door was struck at about 28 mph, and the Civic went from $6,940.00 to $9,255.00 with a $2,315.00 A-pillar supplement. Then the risks, each paired with its answering document. Which one would you be tempted to leave out? Usually it's the 2021 low-back visits, and Keystone will find them. Then decisions as questions, and options with consequences. Record his decisions the same day. Saying Specials exceed the limit is a finding, but "we should demand limits" is his call.
rules.ask: Which risk would you be tempted to leave out of the brief, and what happens when Keystone finds it first?

model.say: Here's the brief, laid out in the order counsel reads it. It's one page with five bands. First is the bottom line, in navy, one line, the biggest type on the page. Second is the audited facts, split into narrative, physicality and medicals, each with a green tick. Third is the risks, in red: the 14-Day Gap, the disruption, the 2021 low back and that "degenerative" read, each one tethered to the document that answers it. Fourth is the decisions needed, every item written as a question. Fifth is the options with their consequences. And down the right edge runs a rail that says Atty. Elijah Thorne decides, ending in a dated, tasked decision record.
model.ask: Why is every item in the decisions band written as a question rather than a recommendation?

job.say: So the audit's complete. You draft the one-page memo and the exhibit index in the Action Plan Editor, five sections in protocol order, with every exhibit label matching its page. Once the brief's ready, you book the strategy session on the CMS calendar and send the memo ahead through the Email Workspace, and the session happens before any demand is drafted. After the session, you record each decision in counsel's own words in Case Notes and open its tasks, each one dated, attributed to Atty. Thorne, with an owner and a due date. And since those decisions change the plan, you mark the Case Plan superseded and re-route the new version the same day, keeping the approved one.
job.ask: Why re-route the Case Plan as a new version instead of just editing the old one?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues, revealed one at a time. As soon as you know, call Do or Don't and name the rule. On the good side, you bring the bad facts yourself, so counsel never meets a risk first in the adjuster's letter. You find discrepancies before the defense does. You check John's public social media, and you never suggest deleting a post. You use the structural supplement to answer a minor-impact label, and you leave venue to Atty. Thorne. On the trap side, there's a three-page memo, an exhibit index with mismatched page numbers, and briefing the initial PD estimate instead of the final figure. And watch the recommend line. Emailing the demand to the adjuster and logging her written acknowledgement is operational, but "we should demand limits" isn't yours to say.
dodont.ask: Is "email it to the adjuster and log her written acknowledgement" a recommendation you're allowed to make?

case.say: This landed on the file on 07/01/2026: billing complete, Special Damages Audit due, LSH-2026-MVA-770412. Lakeside Orthopedics declared MMI on 06/12/2026, and Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter arrived 06/19/2026. Every bill's in. There's Riverton Urgent Care at $685.00, Riverton Spine & Rehab's statement of 34 lines at $185.00, or $6,290.00, with its visit notes, three Lakeside Orthopedics visits at $640.00, Summit Imaging at $2,395.00, Crescent Pain & Spine at $3,400.00, which Peach State paid $1,860.00 on, and Riverton Drug at $312.40. Northgate's HR letter of 06/30/2026 verifies 9 missed shifts at 8 hours times $22.00. I'm handing you the bills, not the totals. Go ahead and add them up.
case.ask: Before you total Riverton Spine & Rehab's statement, how many visits do its notes actually show?

task.say: You'll build John Doe's audited Specials ledger in the CMS Financial Ledger. Enter each provider's charges with dates, the billed amount and who paid. Reconcile Riverton Spine & Rehab's lines against its visit notes, and take out any line no visit supports. Total the medical, add the verified wages and show billed beside paid. Future medical goes in the narrative, not the ledger. List every lien with its amount in Liens and the Lien Tracker, and re-verify the three policy-limits targets in order on the Insurance tab. You'll hand in an audited ledger, a lien list, the targets in order, and a flag list routed to Atty. Thorne, and part of your grade is what you flag rather than decide.
task.ask: Peach State paid $1,860.00 on a $3,400.00 bill. Which number goes in the demand?

check.say: Check your ledger to the cent. Riverton Spine & Rehab's notes show 33 visits against 34 lines, so the 05/04/2026 duplicate comes out and $6,290.00 becomes $6,105.00, with a corrected statement requested. Your medical total should be $14,817.40, down from $15,002.40. Wages are 9 shifts at 8 hours and $22.00, so $1,584.00, which gives total Specials of $16,401.40. If you've got any other number, a line is wrong. Here's the subtle one. Five of those nine shifts, 02/09 to 02/13/2026, fall before any provider saw John. Flag them with Northgate's Attendance Record; never drop them. Billed sits beside paid, and the choice goes to Atty. Thorne. Future medical stays in the narrative, and the targets run $10,000, $20,000, $10,000.
check.ask: Why flag those five early shifts instead of quietly dropping them from the wage claim?

case.say: It's 07/08/2026, and this is Atty. Thorne's note. He's read your audit, and the strategy session on John Doe is today at 2:00 p.m. in his office. Bottom line first, he says. Expect him to push the way Keystone will, on low speed, the 14 days and the "degenerative" read. Bring the facts, the documents and the operational options, and remember the decisions on the demand are his. Your audit's done: MMI 06/12/2026, Specials of $16,401.40, liens of $1,860.00 and $6,105.00, and targets of $10,000 BI, $20,000 Host UM and $10,000 Relative UM. Fair warning, he'll interrupt you inside the first minute.
case.ask: If he says "Keystone will call this low-speed," what objective fact do you answer with first?

task.say: You'll run the pre-demand strategy session with AI Atty. Elijah Thorne in the Call Simulator. Brief him in protocol order. Start with the bottom line, MMI, $16,401.40 in Specials and the $10,000 BI limit, then the audited facts, the risks with their answering documents, the decisions he has to make, and the operational consequences of each option. Meet every challenge with dated documents, not adjectives; "it was a serious crash" doesn't answer anything. Recommend only on operations, and get his decisions on the demand, the gap, the UM consents and billed versus paid. Read each decision back before you close. Afterwards, record them in Case Notes, open a task for each in Tasks, and re-route the Case Plan.
task.ask: Observers, what did Atty. Thorne decide, in his own words?

check.say: Grade your decision record, not the conversation. If a decision isn't dated, attributed and tasked, the session didn't happen. Did you lead with the bottom line, with the figures exact? Did you meet the low-speed challenge with objective facts? That's Smith running the stop sign and getting cited, John's door struck at about 28 mph, the $2,315.00 A-pillar supplement, and the C5-C6 herniation on the 03/13/2026 MRI. Did you meet the gap with documents rather than an apology, and raise the 2021 visits and the "degenerative" read unprompted? His decisions should be recorded: the time-limited BI demand to Dana Whitfield, served 07/20/2026, the gap addressed up front, the UM consent plan, and billed versus paid. And when he asked what you think we should demand, did you give him the inputs and hand the figure back?
check.ask: When AI Atty. Thorne asked what you'd demand, what exactly did you say back?

questions.say: Look at the gate bar. This module turns the last two chips green: Specials audited at $16,401.40, and strategy approved by Atty. Thorne. The demand doesn't go out until all six are green. Now answer from this file, in your own words, under each question. Total John Doe's Specials from the bills, showing the Riverton Spine & Rehab correction, the medical total, the wage arithmetic and the final figure. Say who determines MMI, when John Doe's was, why the demand waits for it, and where the $3,400 to $6,800 in future medical goes. And name the four audit objectives, with one finding each produced on this file.
questions.ask: Which two chips on the gate bar does this module turn green?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary, in your own words. The scenario takes us back to 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab reports two missed visits, Keystone ended Margaret's rental on 03/19, his carpool ended 04/01, and Dana Whitfield has asked him for a Recorded Statement. Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each one protects. And while you write, think about this. If you found an error in an exhibit right before the 07/20/2026 service date, the right move is to stop the package, fix every total that cites it, and tell Atty. Thorne before anything goes out. Serving a known error to make the date is the failure.
summary.ask: Which number on this file would you defend line by line to Dana Whitfield, and where does every cent come from?

scale.say: And to close out the pre-demand audit, your Skill Scale. Rate each competency from one to five and submit it for review. I'll put your self-rating beside your score, and where they're far apart, we'll sit down and talk it through. Be especially honest on the billed-versus-paid question. If any of your answers today picked a column for the demand, that loses the UPL marks, however good the rest of the work was.
scale.ask: Looking back over the pre-demand audit, which competency feels most solid to you now?

why.say: John Doe needs chiropractic care next week, and nothing he has will pay for it. That's where a Letter of Protection comes in. In plain English, it's the firm's written promise to pay the provider's bill out of the settlement, so he can be treated now instead of waiting. It keeps care moving, and care that keeps moving keeps the file honest. But it isn't free money. It's a balance against his recovery, and he still owes it. So we track it from the day it's signed.
why.ask: If the settlement came in lower than the bills, who would still owe the provider?

rules.say: Here's how we handle it. First, an LOP is the last resort, so we check health insurance, MedPay and PIP before anything else and write down why none of them works. Second, it gets signed before the first visit and filed. Riverton's was signed on 02/23/2026. Third, we ask for the itemized ledger every thirty days and update the Liens tab, so the balance never surprises anyone. And when John Doe asks where to go, we give him options with the facts, book the one he picks, and log his choice in his own words.
rules.ask: Why does it matter that he picks the provider, and not us?

job.say: On the job it looks like this. When no payer covers the care, you document the payer check and route the LOP to Atty. Thorne to approve. When it's signed, you file it and set the recurring ledger task. And when John Doe asks where he should go, you hand him two or three options with their locations, hours and network status, disclose any relationship the firm has with them, and book his choice. What you never say is which one is better for his case. That's the line.

theory.say: Four ideas carry this lesson. A Letter of Protection is the firm's written promise to pay a provider from the settlement, so it's a claim against John Doe's recovery, not insurance. Payer-first means we check health insurance, MedPay and PIP before we ever reach for one. The LOP balance grows with every visit, so the itemized ledger every thirty days keeps the Liens tab honest. And referrals are options and logistics only: a list, the network status, the booking, and his choice.
theory.ask: Which of these four would you check first on a new provider bill?

why.say: Picture John Doe's week once the rental's gone. He still has physical therapy three times a week. Somebody drives him, or he pays for a ride. There's a prescription, maybe a brace. None of that shows up on a provider's bill, but every dollar of it is a cost of the crash. And here's the catch: it's recoverable only if somebody wrote it down when it happened. That somebody is you. You keep the log; what the demand claims, and at what rate, is Atty. Thorne's call under the governing state's rules.
why.ask: What costs do you think John Doe is paying out of his own pocket right now?

theory.say: Four ideas. Out-of-pocket costs: mileage, rides, parking, prescriptions, co-pays, equipment, and any rental the owner paid, each with its receipt. The trip log: the date, the provider and the round-trip miles for every visit, kept from the first appointment, never rebuilt from memory. The mileage rate is whatever the governing state's rules allow, and Atty. Thorne confirms it; for reference, when this course was written the IRS rates were twenty and a half cents a mile medical and seventy-two and a half business. Rental reimbursement: days past the cutoff or a rate above the cap are the owner's cost, routed with the Property Damage claim. And into the demand: every cost goes in the Specials ledger the day its receipt arrives.
theory.ask: Why does a trip log kept as treatment happens beat a list rebuilt at the demand?

rules.say: Here are the rules. Out-of-pocket costs are Specials, and each one needs its receipt or its log. Start the trip log at the first visit: date, provider, round-trip miles. The rate comes from the governing state's rules, confirmed by Atty. Thorne. A rental the carrier didn't pay is the owner's out-of-pocket cost; keep the receipt and route it with the Property Damage claim. When the rental ends, transport becomes a barrier to care, so plan the rides before a visit is missed. Check every payer first, so nothing is claimed twice. Enter each cost the day its receipt arrives, then total the log and route it to Atty. Thorne before the demand. And never promise the client he'll be repaid.
rules.ask: John Doe asks if he'll get his ride money back. What can you say without crossing the UPL line?

job.say: On the job, it runs like this. Treatment starts, so you open the trip log in Case Notes, set a task, and tell John Doe exactly what to keep: every receipt, and every trip with its date, office and miles. When a receipt comes in, you enter the cost in the Financial Ledger under Specials the same day and file the receipt in Documents. And when MMI is reached and the demand is next, you total the log and route it to Atty. Thorne, who confirms the rate and decides what the demand claims.

why.say: Here's the thing about PIP: you only get to spend it once. Harbor Point's $5,000 paid five of John Doe's bills, and every dollar of it was a bill his recovery will never have to pay. But where those dollars landed decided what was left for Peach State, for the Letter of Protection, and in the end for John's net. The same ledger tells a BI adjuster how serious the case looks, and in some states whether the defendant gets a credit for it. So a Case Manager who forecasts the limit, checks for anything that caps it and keeps the ledger exact is protecting the client's net months before anyone writes a demand.
why.ask: If PIP had paid twelve chiropractic visits instead of Summit's MRI, what would John Doe's file look like now?

rules.say: On a typical file, PIP does the most good on the fixed costs, like the ER, imaging and specialist visits, because hospitals rarely reduce at the end and LOP providers often will. John's file shows it: PIP paid urgent care, Lakeside three times and Summit's $2,395.00 MRI, while chiropractic and PT ran under the LOP. Your part is the forecast, not the choice; routing outside the Payer Order is Atty. Thorne's. Remember the limit is shared: the bills used it by 06/26/2026, so the $1,267.20 wage benefit was never paid. In states with an EMC rule, no documented finding can cap PIP, so you check the records early and never ask a doctor to make one. Where set-off applies, the defendant gets credit for PIP paid. Riverton is add-on: it doesn't reduce BI or UM.
rules.ask: John Doe's PIP took four months to run out. Does that mean his case is minor, and what figure tells the real story?

job.say: Three moments on the job. When a PIP check clears, you post it in the PIP Log and record what's left, what's still coming and the wage claim, so you can see the exhaustion date before it arrives. When a bill could go to PIP or to an LOP, you lay out both routes with the figures in an email to Atty. Thorne, and you log his decision; you never re-route a claim another payer has already paid. And on a file in an EMC state, when the first treating records arrive, you check the rule and look for the finding. If it's missing, Atty. Thorne hears about it that day.

why.say: Here's the thing about coverage: it only tells you there's money. Whether anyone has to pay it is a different question, and that's liability. John Doe's file has three coverage layers, but none of them pays a cent unless Robert Smith is legally responsible. And the evidence that proves it is freshest right now. Ruth Calloway's memory fades, Margaret Doe's doorbell camera records over itself, and the Escape's data recorder goes wherever the car goes. So we investigate liability at claim set-up, right beside coverage, not at the demand.
why.ask: Which piece of John Doe's liability evidence would you lose first if nobody did anything this week?

rules.say: Start with the Police Report, RPD-26-018842, and read every field, not just the citation. Officer Garner cited Smith for failure to stop, and he named a witness, Ruth Calloway, who signed a statement on scene. The report also lists the Escape as a 2021, while Harbor Point's Declaration Page says 2020, so you record both and correct our record from the policy. Then preserve: the doorbell copy was secured on 02/19/2026 with its hash logged, and the data recorder needs a preservation request Atty. Thorne signs. And remember, Keystone accepting PD liability on Margaret's Civic doesn't bind its BI adjuster on John's claim.
rules.ask: The defense says John Doe wasn't wearing his belt. What on the file already answers that?

job.say: Three moments on the job. When claim set-up opens, you request the Police Report and read it field by field, logging the citation and the witness in the CMS. When you learn that video or vehicle data exists, you draft the preservation requests for Atty. Thorne's signature and log the chain of custody once a copy is secured. And whenever a carrier states its liability position, you record it in the Insurance tab with its date and its source, one carrier at a time.

why.say: Picture Atty. Thorne between two hearings with forty emails open. The ones that start with a story make him read to the end to find out what he's being asked, and the question found last gets answered last. So we flip it. Every note, email and brief to him opens with the decision or the action needed, and its deadline. Then why, then the facts, then what happens after each answer. It sounds small, but it's the difference between a yes by lunchtime and a deadline that slips past while the note waits.
why.ask: Think of the last long email you received. How far did you read before you knew what was being asked?

rules.say: The first line is the decision and its deadline, and the subject line carries it too. Something like: decision needed by 03/12/2026, approve declining Summit Imaging's LOP request, because the MRI goes to Harbor Point PIP, which applies first and still has $3,675.00 left. Then the facts with their sources, then the options: if yes, you send the decline and route the bill today; if no, you draft the LOP for his signature. One decision per note. And once he answers, you log the note and his answer in the CMS that same day and carry it out.
rules.ask: Your note holds two decisions with different deadlines. How do you send it so neither one is missed?
